name: Hearth
description: Hearth brings your services, your infrastructure, and an AI administrator together in one place. Ember, its AI, looks after your homelab with you: it investigates, explains, and fixes things through plans you approve.
status: In active development. Not available to download yet.

emberLoop.note: Talk or type, in plain words.
Reads logs, app status, and your machine through Hearth's own tools.
Explains what is wrong and how sure it is.
Proposes an exact plan, step by step.
You choose what needs your OK: every change, risky steps, or only steps with serious consequences.
Installs, restarts, repairs, and settings in any connected app, as the plan you approved.
Each step is checked by reading the result back, and the plan stops at the first failure. Changed settings are put back; anything that can't be undone is marked before you approve.
Keeps what it learned, with you reviewing what it saves.

screens.title: Sonarr, explained
screens.caption: Stuck and failed downloads named with the app's own reason, and one-click Import or Search, each a plan you approve.

screens.title: You approve the exact plan
screens.caption: A separate example: a two-step plan that checks Jellyfin, then restarts it. Each step says how it will be checked and what happens if a later step fails. Approval covers this plan, once.

screens.title: Home
screens.caption: Ember, the AI, in the middle, your active projects around it, what needs you in one row, and your homelab's vital signs below. All on one screen.

screens.title: The Lair: a panel for each app
screens.caption: Open any app beside Ember. With branding on, each panel wears its app's own colors. qBittorrent shows stalled and broken torrents first, each with the repairs that fit it.

screens.title: Who is watching what
screens.caption: Plex libraries and live streams: direct play or transcode, buffering, and an Ask Ember button on every stream.

screens.title: Storage & Files
screens.caption: Every drive with its health and temperature, plus files, recent downloads, file journeys, and RAID arrays.

screens.title: The War Room
screens.caption: Your projects with Claude Code, Codex, or a local Ollama model: a terminal, a task queue, files, and a kill switch.

screens.title: Notifications
screens.caption: Email, Discord, ntfy, or a webhook. Hearth writes only when something matters and says whether you need to act.

screens.title: Make Ember your own
screens.caption: Rename your AI, pick a built-in voice or your own speech machine, and choose how much it may do on its own.

screens.title: Plan your first homelab
screens.caption: Pick what sounds fun in plain words. Hearth looks at your computer, only if you say yes, and explains every option.

screens.title: A plan that fits your computer
screens.caption: Every app explained: what it does, why it was picked, what it costs, and whether it runs comfortably on your machine.

screens.title: A home dashboard for your wall
screens.caption: Hearth turns Home Assistant into a full-screen dashboard for a wall tablet or a spare screen: the time written out, the weather with a sky that matches outside, what's playing, today's calendar, shopping lists and scenes.

screens.title: The forecast, one tap away
screens.caption: The next hours and the next days, from Home Assistant or a free weather service for your town.

screens.title: The same home on your phone
screens.caption: Pair a phone or tablet and it opens straight to the home dashboard, with Rooms, Media, Security and Household a tap away.

screens.title: Tell friends what is new
screens.caption: When a movie or show lands in Plex or Jellyfin, Hearth posts it to your friends' Discord with its poster, details and trailer. Shown with Night of the Living Dead (1968, public domain).

screens.title: Watch parties, with a banner
screens.caption: The Banner style: Hearth draws the title, time and your note over the movie's own backdrop, with its poster beside them, then the RSVP card. Night of the Living Dead (1968, public domain).

screens.title: Pick the look
screens.caption: Banner, Cinematic, Streaming, or Compact. Streaming puts the movie's backdrop under the invitation. Friends answer I'm in or Can't make it.

screens.title: Planned, with a guest list
screens.caption: The watch party, who is coming, and spots left. Change the time, add a room code, or cancel it, and everyone invited hears about it.

screens.title: Add Discord in one click
screens.caption: Add a destination, choose the Hearth bot, and pick who reads it. A friends and family channel only ever gets media announcements, never system alerts.

screens.title: The Hearth bot, no token needed
screens.caption: Add Hearth to your Discord server, pick the channel, and you are done. Movie night invitations get I'm in and Can't make it buttons.

screens.title: Or use your own Discord bot
screens.caption: Prefer your own? Set it up step by step in about two minutes. Its token goes into Hearth's vault and is never shown again.

pricing.title: Free for your home, with a few paid add-ons
pricing.lead: Hearth is free for personal and home use. Two optional add-ons will cost extra, and businesses need a licence. We're saying so now, before anyone downloads it.
free: Everything a single Hearth does: Ember, a panel for each app, monitoring, the vault, plans you approve, backups and undo.
As many phones, tablets and wall screens as you like, paired to your Hearth.
As many separate Hearths as you like, one on each PC.
Your own AI: Claude Code, Codex, or a local model through Ollama, at no cost from us.
paid: Link your Hearths on different PCs so they work as one, with every PC's projects and systems in one place. Paid from the first link.
While Hearth's AI works, it opens and points at what it is examining, and Teach me explains why it matters. The AI does the same work without it.
pricing.business: Businesses, consultants, and anyone using Hearth to make money will need a business licence.
pricing.note: Prices aren't set yet. Once a feature ships free, it never moves behind a payment.

emberIntro: Ember is Hearth's AI. It doesn't stop at answering questions: it looks into what's really happening on your machines, explains it in plain words, and fixes things.

Ember is the AI you connect: Claude Code, Codex, or a local model through Ollama, with everything that AI can do. Hearth doesn't hold it back. You only decide what it asks your permission for before it acts.

You pick one of three: ask before every change (the default), ask before risky steps like restarts, app settings, or installs, or ask only before steps with serious consequences, like deleting data, changing networking, or using sudo. Ember asks in its reply and goes on after you say yes.

workflow.title: One fix, start to finish
workflow.intro: A real run in a development build, using sample data: a download Sonarr left behind, the exact change Hearth proposes, and the check afterwards.

steps.title: 1. The problem
steps.caption: The Sonarr panel lists finished downloads Sonarr hasn't imported. Sonarr matched one file to The Copper Line, season 2 episode 7; the other it couldn't place, so it waits for you.

steps.title: 2. The exact plan
steps.caption: Nothing moves yet. The plan names the file, where it goes, and how: moved into the show, not copied.

steps.title: 3. Checked afterwards
steps.caption: After you approve, Hearth reads Sonarr back to confirm the episode has its file. An import isn't undone automatically; a wrong one is removed in Sonarr.

workflow.note: This fix started from the Sonarr panel. When Ember proposes a fix in chat, it comes as the same kind of plan for you to approve.
